title: How to plot a land title technical description | Spatialdom Insights
description: A practical reading workflow for plotting bearings and distances from a Philippine land title, checking closure, and knowing when to ask a geodetic engineer.
heading: How to plot a land title technical description
intro: A plot turns a list of boundary calls into a shape you can inspect. Start with the source document, follow the lines in order, and treat any mismatch as a question to investigate.

sections.heading: Prepare the source
paragraphs: Use a legible technical description and, if available, the approved survey plan. Record the lot and plan identifiers, the point of beginning, each line's bearing and distance, and the unit shown. Keep the source beside the plot so every entry can be checked.

Separate the tie line from the parcel boundary. A tie point helps locate the lot relative to a reference; the boundary calls describe the lot's shape. Drawing only the boundary can help you understand the shape, but it does not establish its position on the ground.

sections.heading: Trace and check the lines
paragraphs: Begin at the first lot corner. Enter each bearing and distance in the order written, moving from the end of one line to the start of the next. Check the quadrant letters, degrees, minutes, seconds, decimal places, and units before proceeding.

After the final line, compare the drawing with the plan and check whether the path returns to its starting point. If it does not, first recheck transcription, omitted lines, and point order. A mismatch in a quick plot is not proof that the title or survey is wrong.

sections.heading: Know what the plot can answer
paragraphs: A plot can expose an unexpected shape or a line that deserves a closer look. It cannot confirm ownership, title validity, physical monuments, or an official boundary. For a decision about a property, compare the relevant official records and ask a licensed geodetic engineer to review material discrepancies.

candidate.description: A practical Philippine guide to turning a land title technical description into a parcel sketch, checking the result, and knowing what the plot can and cannot prove.
candidate.heading: How to plot a land title technical description
candidate.intro: A technical description is a sequence of directions and distances around a parcel. Plotting it is useful because it turns dense text into a shape you can inspect—but the drawing is still an interpretation of the document, not a field survey or proof of where the boundary lies on the ground.

sections.heading: Start with the source, not the software
paragraphs: Before plotting anything, identify exactly what document you are reading. On Philippine survey records and titles, the useful clues usually include the lot number, survey plan number, location, area, tie point, and the sequence of boundary lines. If you also have the approved survey plan or lot data computation, keep it beside the title. The goal is not simply to make a polygon appear; it is to preserve the meaning of the source while you encode it.

This matters because a technical description may contain both a tie line and the parcel boundary. The tie line connects a known reference point to a lot corner. The boundary calls then trace the parcel itself. If you accidentally treat the tie line as one side of the property, the drawing can look plausible while being conceptually wrong.

sections.heading: Read each boundary call as one movement
paragraphs: A boundary call tells you two things: direction and distance. For example, a line written as N 35° 20' E, 24.50 m means travel 24.50 meters in a direction 35 degrees 20 minutes east of north. The next line begins where that line ends. Continue in the order written until the final boundary call returns toward the first corner.

Copy quadrant letters, degrees, minutes, seconds, decimals, and units exactly. N 35° E is not interchangeable with S 35° E, and a missed digit in a distance can noticeably distort the lot. When a title is old, photocopied, scanned, or typed from another record, transcription deserves as much attention as the plotting itself.

sections.heading: Separate parcel shape from parcel location
paragraphs: There are two different questions hidden inside a technical description: what shape does this sequence produce, and where does that shape belong geographically? Bearings and distances can reconstruct the parcel geometry from an arbitrary starting corner. That is enough for a useful first look at shape, area, and closure.

Placing the parcel on a map requires more information. DENR procedures for cadastral data distinguish boundary bearings and distances from the control or tie information used to derive coordinates, and Geoportal Philippines' lot plotter likewise asks for a tie point before locating a lot. A parcel can therefore be drawn correctly as a shape without yet being reliably georeferenced.

sections.heading: Check whether the parcel closes—but do not stop there
paragraphs: After the last line, compare the final point with the starting point. If they meet within the precision expected from the source, the traverse closes. If there is a gap, go back through the original text before assuming the underlying survey is wrong. Common causes include a reversed quadrant, a missing line, a decimal error, wrong point order, or a tie line entered as a boundary.

Closure is a useful internal check, not a certificate of correctness. A wrong sequence can sometimes still form a closed shape. Likewise, a parcel may close while being attached to the wrong reference point or placed using an inappropriate coordinate system. Treat closure as one diagnostic among several.

sections.heading: Use the plot to ask better questions
paragraphs: A quick plot is excellent for seeing whether the parcel is long and narrow, irregular, unexpectedly large, or obviously different from the plan you expected. It can also help you identify the exact line that deserves rechecking. This is where a tool such as Parcel Plotter is most useful: it shortens the path from technical text to something a landowner, buyer, broker, student, or professional can inspect.

What it cannot do is verify ownership, authenticate the title, recover missing monuments, settle a boundary dispute, or replace a relocation or other professional land survey. Philippine law places land surveys, determination of metes and bounds, subdivision and consolidation work, and related survey plans within the practice of Geodetic Engineering. If the result will affect a purchase, construction, subdivision, legal dispute, or actual occupation on the ground, have the relevant records reviewed by a licensed Geodetic Engineer.
